items.title: Blockbuster could have bought Netflix for $50 million in 2000
items.claim: In 2000, Netflix was a struggling DVD-by-mail service. What did Blockbuster's CEO John Antioco do when Reed Hastings flew to Dallas to propose a sale?

options.text: Agreed in principle but the deal collapsed over terms
Laughed Hastings out of the room
Counter-offered to buy Netflix for $200 million
Bought a minority stake to monitor the technology

items.reveal_title: The room where it didn't happen
items.reveal:
Reed Hastings and Marc Randolph have both told the story (Randolph's book 'That Will Never Work' has the most colour). They proposed Blockbuster acquire Netflix for $50 million and run blockbuster.com as the online arm. Antioco — facing a profitable late-fee business model — declined.

Blockbuster did later launch an online service (Blockbuster Online) and was on a recovery path under Antioco, but a 2005 boardroom fight with activist investor Carl Icahn led to Antioco's departure and the strategy's reversal. Blockbuster filed for bankruptcy in 2010.

Netflix's market cap is now over $300 billion.
items.why: Disruption isn't usually about technology incumbents can't access; it's about business models they can't bring themselves to attack. Late fees were too profitable to risk.

items.title: Taylor's piece rate was an incentive, not a wage
items.claim: F.W. Taylor at Bethlehem Steel in the 1890s introduced piece-rate pay. What was the central design feature?

options.text: All workers received the same base pay regardless of output
Workers were paid per unit produced, with the 'scientific' target set so only those following Taylor's prescribed method could earn the bonus
Piece rates were determined by union negotiation

items.reveal_title: Pay per piece, conditional on method
items.reveal:
Taylor's pig-iron handling experiments at Bethlehem Steel (1898-99) raised loading from 12.5 to 47 tons per worker per day. Workers earning the bonus received about 60% more pay; the firm got 280% more output per worker.

Unions opposed Taylorism fiercely — 1911 US Congressional hearings investigated 'speed-up' abuses. Modern piece rates persist in garment factories, gig economy (Uber surge pricing as a variant) and sales commissions.
items.why: Piece rates align effort with output but can erode quality, safety and worker autonomy. The same design principle reappears in 'pay for performance' compensation a century later.

items.title: Demographics often predict less than marketers assume
items.claim: Mark Ritson and others have argued that traditional demographic segmentation (age, income, gender) often performs poorly. What's the evidence?

options.text: Demographics predict purchase behaviour with high accuracy
Within-group variation in purchase behaviour is often larger than between-group variation; behavioural segmentation (what people actually buy) typically outperforms demographic segmentation
Demographics are legally required for marketing
Segmentation has been abandoned in modern marketing

items.reveal:
Byron Sharp's 'How Brands Grow' (2010), drawing on the Ehrenberg-Bass Institute, argued that mass-market brands grow through reach, not narrow targeting — and that demographic targeting often misallocates spend. Coca-Cola buyers, Toyota buyers and HSBC customers look broadly similar demographically.

Behavioural segmentation (heavy vs light buyers, lapsed vs active) typically explains more variance. Geographic and psychographic add incremental power.
items.why: Marketing teaching often defaults to demographic segmentation because it's easy to teach and the data is available. The evidence suggests it's a weaker guide than is taught.
